item.title: Spring Web Application: Differentiating applicationContext XML and servlet-specific Contexts
item.description:
“Spring Web Application: Differentiating applicationContext XML and servlet-specific Contexts”

When building Spring web applications, developers often utilize multiple ApplicationContext configurations. The standard pattern involves a root context, typically loaded via applicationContext.xml, and one or more servlet-specific contexts, often named like *-servlet.xml (e.g., spring-servlet.xml or myApp-servlet.xml), which are bound to a DispatcherServlet.

What precisely dictates the purpose and scope of beans defined in these distinct configuration files, and how do they interact within the lifecycle of a running web application deployed on a servlet container like Tomcat?

item.title: Troubleshooting Spring's NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: Causes and Solutions
item.description:
“Troubleshooting Spring’s NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: Causes and Solutions”

Let’s delve into the typical scenarios that lead to this exception and how to effectively resolve them.

What is a BeanFactory in Spring?

At its core, a BeanFactory is the abstraction representing Spring’s Inversion of Control (IoC) container. It’s responsible for managing the lifecycle of beans and exposing them to your application. When the container cannot find or retrieve a requested bean, it raises a NoSuchBeanDefinitionException.

item.title: Solved: How to fix NullPointerException with @Autowired in Spring Framework
item.description:
“Solved: How to fix NullPointerException with @Autowired in Spring Framework”

At its core, the Spring IoC container acts as a sophisticated manager for your application’s components, often referred to as “beans.” It maintains a registry of these beans (ApplicationContext), configures their properties by injecting dependencies, and orchestrates their creation in the correct order. The crucial point is that the IoC container needs to be aware of an object for it to perform autowiring. If you create an object yourself using the new operator, Spring bypasses its configuration process, leaving any @Autowired fields uninitialized and thus null.
